evidence.text: Phonosemantic compound. 艹 represents the meaning and 余 represents the sound.

evidence.source: wiktionary
evidence.text:
Phono-semantic compound (形聲 /形声, OC *rlaː): semantic 艹 + phonetic 余 (OC *la).
茶, then slightly modified into a more conservative 茶, originates as a graphical modification of archaic 荼 (*rlaː, “bitter plant”), used for “tea” in classical sources. The modern version is unrelated to the bottom component of 條.
As tea may have originated from Sichuan, where the native Yi people speak Loloish languages, Sagart (1999) suggests that the Old Chinese item was possibly originally borrowed from Proto-Loloish *la¹ (“tea”), from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-la (“leaf; tea”). Schuessler (2007) traces its ultimate origin to Proto-Austroasiatic *slaʔ (“leaf”) (in Sidwell's 2024 reconstruction).
Alternatively, Qiu (1988) suggests that it might be a semantic extension of 荼 (*rlaː, “bitter plant”).

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi, as transcribed and annotated by Shuowen.cn
evidence.text: The entry is for 荼, not the later graph 茶: it glosses it as 苦荼 and analyzes it as 艸 (plant category) plus 余 as phonetic. This supports a phonetic role for 余 in 荼; it does not establish that every stroke in the later 茶 is a meaningful component.
evidence.title: 说文解字：茶／荼

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database describes 茶 as a later graph, written earlier with 艸 and phonetic 余 as 荼. It gives 茶 as tea plant and tea drink, and cites Lu Yu’s Tang-period 茶經, which calls tea a fine southern tree. It also records later uses for other brewed drinks and, in Ming usage, as a verb ‘drink’. These glosses do not by themselves date each semantic extension.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：茶

evidence.source: Zhang Yongmei, Essays on Linguistics (Peking University Journals)
evidence.text: The 2025 abstract argues that in the Shijing period only 荼 occurred and it did not mean tea; it assigns 荼 a tea sense and reading *deɑ by the Western Han at the latest, with 茶 appearing as a graphic derivative used alongside 荼 for tea. It argues the distinction developed gradually: Tang Buddhist texts show the tea reading of 荼 fading, 茶 increasingly replaced 荼 after mid-Tang, and later Ming dictionaries completed the separation. This is a recent scholarly account, not settled primary evidence; the page provides only an abstract.
evidence.title: “荼”与“茶”表茗茶的形音义源流试探

evidence.source: Victor Mair, Language Log
evidence.text: Mair argues medieval manuscript forms vary in their lower strokes and that 茶 was not necessarily an independent replacement of 荼 at first. In his account, surviving Qieyun manuscript evidence around 700 CE generally writes the tea plant with a graph transcribed as 荼; a 706 CE manuscript gives no 茶 form in its cited line, while a reading that mentions 茶 in another manuscript requires image verification. He reports Guangyun (1007 CE) lists 茶 as俗 relative to the regular form. He also cautions that a Han tomb seal often read 茶陵 may instead read 荼陵. This challenges simple claims that 茶 was securely established in Han times or invented by Lu Yu.
evidence.title: Sinographs for “tea”

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: For 茶 the database gives Guangyun fanqie 宅加 and Middle Chinese classification 澄母, level tone, open division II, 麻 rhyme. This is a Middle Chinese system/classification, distinct from the Old Chinese reconstructions in the dossier. It supports comparison with a historical reading of the whole character but the page does not independently supply a matching reconstructed pronunciation for 余.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：茶

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003)
evidence.text: The entry lists 余 at Old Chinese *la and 茶 at Old Chinese *rlaː in Zhengzhang’s reconstruction. These are readings within the same named reconstruction system and make a plausible historical sound-component comparison. The page is a tertiary compilation; this does not independently establish the earliest shape or referent of 余.

evidence.source: National Palace Museum, Monthly of Chinese Art, issue 494 (May 2024)
evidence.text: The article notes that Wang Bao’s Western Han 僮約 contains 烹荼盡具 and 武都買荼, often treated as early evidence for tea drinking, but explicitly says whether that 荼 denotes tea remains disputed. It distinguishes those textual references from Huayang guozhi passages that identify tea as a product of Shu. Thus the Han text is an early candidate attestation, not an uncontested proof of the tea sense.

evidence.source: Wiktionary, summarizing Sagart (1999), Schuessler (2007), and Qiu (1988)
evidence.text: The page reports competing proposals for the spoken tea word: a possible Old Chinese loan from Proto-Loloish *la¹ ‘tea’, possibly related to Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-la ‘leaf; tea’; an ultimate Proto-Austroasiatic *slaʔ ‘leaf’ source attributed to Schuessler; or a semantic extension of 荼 ‘bitter plant’ attributed to Qiu. These are alternatives concerning the word, not graphic formation. The inspected material does not independently establish the source-language pronunciation or the borrowing pathway, so no proposal can be preferred here.
